reasons.reason: Imported capital goods are inputs for domestic firms, so when the weaker currency makes them pricier, the cost of producing every unit rises and firms supply less at each price level, pulling short-run supply leftward.

Capital goods are long-lived investment purchases, not the variable inputs that set short-run costs, so a pricier import changes spending and the price level, which shows up as a movement along short-run supply rather than a shift.
When rates are already near the floor, bond prices are sitting at their peak and offer little upside, so nobody wants to buy them and the central bank's purchases cannot push yields down any further.
At a very low rate people will hold any extra money the central bank creates instead of buying bonds, so the money demand curve goes flat and added money supply leaves the interest rate where it was.

A recessionary gap often comes with inflation fears from earlier stimulus, and pulling money out of circulation steadies prices and confidence so that spending can recover on a sound footing rather than on cheap credit.

A recessionary gap means output is below potential because spending is too weak, and the direct fiscal fix is for government to add its own purchases, which raises aggregate demand and gets multiplied through the economy.

A tax cut leaves households with more disposable income, so consumption rises, firms respond by producing more to meet that demand, and the economy's measured output goes up as people put in extra hours.
At full employment there is no spare capacity, so when the tax cut raises consumer spending, firms cannot produce much more and the extra demand mostly bids prices up instead of output.

Selling a corporate building is a large market transaction with a price paid in the current year, and GDP is built from the market value of transactions, so that sale gets recorded in the national accounts.

GDP counts final goods produced this year, and business purchases of newly made machinery and equipment are the investment component of spending, unlike transfers, resales or financial asset purchases that create no new output.

Cheaper foreign imports pull domestic buyers toward foreign goods and away from home-produced ones, and with less spending on the country's own output, the world needs less of its currency to pay for it.
Foreign investors hold a currency to earn its interest, so once domestic rates fall below what the rest of the world pays, they move funds elsewhere and need less of this currency.

A drop in the foreign currency's price against ours shifts trade terms in favor of the domestic side, and foreigners respond to that shift by buying more of our goods, which is what the exchange change sets off.
A cheaper foreign currency means each unit of it buys fewer units of ours, so domestic goods cost foreigners more in their own money and they cut back on what they buy from us.
Shrinking the money supply raises interest rates, and higher borrowing costs feed straight into firms' expenses, which they pass on as higher prices, so the central bank's move lifts the price level.

Cutting the money supply pushes interest rates up, which makes borrowing for investment and big purchases costlier, so total spending falls and the economy's demand curve moves inward to cool things down.
Nominal means stated in a fixed reference unit, so nominal GDP is the version corrected to base-year terms, while real GDP is the raw figure actually recorded in today's currency.
Real GDP values output at constant base-year prices, stripping out price changes so it tracks quantities, while nominal GDP uses current prices and so moves with inflation as well as output.
Optimistic consumers start spending ahead of their expected income, which drives up prices, and with a higher price level the real value of money falls, so the quantity of output demanded shrinks.

Higher personal income taxes leave households with less disposable income, so consumption falls at every price level, and since consumption is the biggest piece of total spending, the demand curve moves left.

Long-run supply reflects the economy's productive capacity, and a higher labor force participation rate means more workers available at full employment, so potential output grows and the vertical curve moves right.
A higher price level raises the revenue firms earn on each unit, and over time that sustained profitability draws in new firms and capacity, so the economy's long-run productive potential expands.
Government spending carries a multiplier, so each extra dollar of purchases generates several dollars of income and production as it circulates, which adds substantially to the economy's real output.
With the economy already at full employment, output cannot rise much further, so the extra government demand competes for the same workers and resources and mostly drives up prices instead.

Cost-push inflation comes from rising wages and input prices, and higher wages give workers more to spend, so firms see stronger sales and ramp up production, which lifts real output during the episode.
Cost-push inflation starts on the supply side, when input costs like wages or oil rise, so firms produce less at each price level and short-run supply moves left, raising prices while output falls.
The spending multiplier comes from how much of each dollar gets re-spent, so with consumption at 0.8 it works out to one over 0.8, which is 1.25, and that times the $100 million gives the total.
The spending multiplier is one over one minus the marginal propensity to consume, so with 0.8 that is one over 0.2, which is 5, and 5 times the $100 million gives the total change.
A sphere fitted inside a solid takes up two-thirds of that solid's volume, and the cone here has volume one-third times pi times 36 times 8, which is 96 pi, so two-thirds of that is 64 pi.

In the cross-section the slant side is 10, and the incircle radius is the triangle's area over its semiperimeter, 48 over 16, which is 3, so the sphere's volume is four-thirds pi times 27, giving 36 pi.
